# Working hypotheses

**These are claims, not findings.** They were generated by analysing the record in `evidence-log.md`. None has been tested. They are listed with their unresolved objections attached, and they are ranked by how much the existing evidence supports them — not by how interesting they are.

If you are reading this repository for the evidence record, that is `evidence-log.md`. Nothing there depends on anything here.

---

## 1. The two-hit model

Attacks appear to require **both** an inherited vulnerable vessel wall **and** an open hypothalamic timing window. Neither alone is sufficient.

The vessel-wall side: risk genes are artery-enriched (Analysis 2), risk alleles change gene expression mainly in arteries (Analysis 5), and the drug targets of treatments that work are artery-enriched. The timing side: attacks are strongly circadian and seasonal, and provocation agents reliably fail during remission — the same chemical trigger that induces an attack in an active bout does nothing between bouts.

**Prediction.** Combining a vessel drug (verapamil) with a clock drug beats either alone.

## 2. Multiple trigger routes converge

CGRP, PACAP, VIP and KATP-channel opening each provoke attacks in active-bout patients. Blocking one route should therefore be insufficient, which is consistent with the mixed CGRP-antibody results. PACAP may act on both hits — VPAC receptors on vessels, PAC1 in the hypothalamus — while VIP looks vessel-only.

## 3. 5-HT7 blockade

*Rewritten after Analysis 6, which reversed the direction of the original version of this hypothesis.*

Every drug reported to end a cluster bout — methysergide, dihydroergotamine, ergotamine, BOL-148 — is a 5-HT7 **antagonist**. Frovatriptan, which has shown no lasting effect, is a full **agonist**. 5-HT7 potency separates bout-enders from attack-stoppers by about elevenfold (pKi 7.67 vs 6.65; exact permutation p = 0.067, which is the floor at n = 6, and the observed ordering is the single most extreme of the 15 possible).

HTR7 ranks first of 514 background genes on joint artery-and-hypothalamus tissue specificity — the only candidate sitting in both halves of the two-hit model. No cluster headache risk gene is dual; they are artery-only. 5-HT7 is also the serotonergic receptor through which circadian phase resetting runs: knockout mice lose non-photic shifts, and the selective antagonist JNJ-18038683 blunts both photic and non-photic phase shifts.

No paper has ever paired 5-HT7 with cluster headache.

A compound exists. JNJ-18038683 is selective, completed Phase 2 in 285 patients across major depression and bipolar disorder, was tolerated, missed both efficacy endpoints, and was shelved. REM latency serves as a human target-engagement biomarker.

### Objection (a): 5-HT2A cannot be separated

Every drug with any cluster headache report blocks 5-HT2A harder than 5-HT7 — chlorpromazine 8.1 vs 7.6, olanzapine 8.9 vs 6.5. HTR2A is second on the dual-tissue measure. And lurasidone, the most potent 5-HT7 blocker in the curated set at pKi 9.3, has zero cluster headache reports. On these data 5-HT7 may simply be along for the ride.

### Objection (b): blockade may lift a brake on CGRP

Prejunctional 5-HT7 **activation** inhibits perivascular CGRP release — the release galcanezumab works downstream of. A pure 5-HT7 antagonist would block cranial vasodilation and remove that brake simultaneously, with an unknown net effect.

### The refined claim, which survives both objections

The bout-ending profile is **5-HT1B/1D/1F agonism plus 5-HT7 antagonism**, not 5-HT7 blockade alone. The ergots and BOL-148 have both. Triptans have the first without much of the second. JNJ-18038683 and lurasidone have the second without the first.

**Decisive test.** A 5-HT1 agonist alone versus the same agonist plus 5-HT7 blockade.
**Separating test.** A selective 5-HT7 antagonist versus a selective 5-HT2A antagonist in the existing levcromakalim provocation model.
**Cheapest first experiment.** Measure CGRP release from cranial tissue under 5-HT7 blockade. This settles objection (b) and needs only an assay that already exists in working labs.

## 4. Vascular-selective KATP blockade

Levcromakalim, a KATP opener, provokes attacks. The vascular channel subtype is Kir6.1/SUR2B (KCNJ8/ABCC9), which is distinct from the neuronal and pancreatic subtypes. Selective blockade of the vascular subtype is an entirely untested treatment class.

## 5. Placebo rates hide real effects in episodic trials

Placebo responder rates of 37–53% are routine, because episodic bouts end on their own. Episodic trials are therefore underpowered in a way sample size alone doesn't fix. Prefer chronic populations, longer baselines, and crossover designs within the same patient.

## 6. Episodic and chronic are different diseases for trial purposes

nVNS and galcanezumab both worked in episodic and failed in chronic. Pooling them obscures real effects in both directions.

## 7. Timing may matter more than dose

Effective preventives converge on circadian modulation. Candidates: timed melatonin, ramelteon, tasimelteon, timed light. Counter-evidence: a 2022 mouse study found verapamil, lithium and prednisone produced no anterior hypothalamic clock-gene change. Analysis 6 supplies a mechanism this hypothesis previously lacked — 5-HT7 blockade blunts phase shifting — but that is a hypothesis about a hypothesis.

## 8. Pre-emptive prevention has never been tried

Every episodic prevention trial requires an active bout to enrol. Nobody has tested starting treatment *before* an expected bout, despite the seasonal predictability that makes it feasible. Two case reports of galcanezumab started pre-bout are suggestive and nothing more.

## 9. DOWNGRADED — PLCE1 genotype and lithium response

The original idea was that lithium offsets overactive PLCE1 signalling. Analysis 5 showed the risk alleles **lower** PLCE1 expression, which is the opposite of the premise. Still testable pharmacogenetically in existing genotyped cohorts, but no longer a priority.

## 10. Hypothalamic–gonadal axis

Clomiphene interrupted chronicity in a 15-patient case series and produced a multi-year remission in a case report. Never placebo-controlled. Deserves a pilot.

## 11. Oxygen's mechanism is unknown

A rat model points to parasympathetic rather than trigeminal action; a healthy-volunteer study found no effect on the provoked autonomic reflex; CPAP failed outright. For the most effective acute treatment in the disease, this is a conspicuous gap.

## 12. The antipsychotic reports were never followed up

Chlorpromazine relieved 12 of 13 patients in a 1980 open series. Olanzapine aborted attacks in 4 of 5. There is one clozapine case report. These drugs are unsuitable for routine prevention because of their side effects, but they are the only human hint that blocking the 5-HT7/5-HT2A pair does anything in cluster headache — and the observation has sat unexamined for forty-five years.

---

## Open questions

Each is a piece of work rather than an argument.

- Does blocking 5-HT7 in cranial tissue raise or lower CGRP release?
- Can 5-HT7 be separated from 5-HT2A with existing tool compounds?
- Has any 5-HT1B/1D/1F agonist plus 5-HT7 antagonist combination ever been given to humans?
- Is JNJ-18038683 obtainable by an academic group?
- What cluster headache patient-reported data already exists, and has anyone analysed it?

## Analyses not yet run

- [ ] Single-cell mapping across hypothalamus, trigeminal ganglion and vascular smooth muscle — needs a reachable single-cell atlas API
- [ ] Patient-report text mining for treatment-outcome signals
- [ ] Drug-target Mendelian randomisation — blocked on the Winsvold 2023 summary statistics, which are not public
- [ ] UK and German funding, properly queried
